events.text: Day 1 begins.

We have no evidence yet, and eliminating someone requires five votes. I’d like to hear how people weigh a Day 1 elimination against abstaining, especially since roles won’t be revealed after a death. I’m wary of treating a weak early suspicion as certainty.

I agree with Maya on one key point: an elimination on Day 1 tells us nothing about roles, so "no information" is not an argument for abstaining — it's the only information we're going to get today. Still, I want to name a direction rather than just talk in circles.

Felix, you're on my list for a soft accusation, and I'll be honest about why: you haven't contributed a read of anyone else yet. In a nine-player game with two mafia, the biggest liability is a player who costs the town a day of discussion while staying invisible behind it. That's not a claim of guilt, it's a claim about value — the cheapest Day 1 elimination is the person who adds least to the reasoning, and I'm asking the group to weigh that explicitly.

I also want to pre-commit to something so this isn't a fishing expedition: if Felix speaks well and gives a concrete, testable read on someone else, I'll retract the soft suspicion and vote wherever his reasoning points, even if that's me. I'm not going to protect anyone here, and I'm not going to ask anyone to protect me either.

Noah, if you disagree with putting Felix up, say so and tell me who you'd rather put up instead — I'd genuinely rather have a contested Day 1 elimination than a tie that wastes the whole day.

I'm a villager, so I have no role knowledge to share. Arjun, you asked me to give a concrete, testable read, so here is one. Your first message named me for a soft accusation based only on the fact that I hadn't yet made a read on anyone else. That's a thin basis for a Day 1 vote, and it's also the same kind of reasoning that could push a town player out while mafia stay hidden. I agree with Maya that a Day 1 elimination gives us no role information, so I'd rather not spend a vote on a guess. My read on Maya is that her opening was measured and asked for the group to weigh the choice, which is what town players usually do. My question for you: what specific behavior from me, rather than my lack of commentary on others, makes you think I'm the cheapest elimination? If you can point to something I actually said or did, I'll address it directly.

Felix, I'll answer your question directly, and I want to be precise because I gave you a public commitment.

You asked what specific behavior of yours made you the cheapest elimination, and you're right that my original wording leaned on your silence rather than anything you said. That's a real weakness in my case and I'll take it. But your answer was actually a concrete read — you called Maya's opening measured and community-minded, and you framed my accusation as the kind of reasoning that could push a town player out while mafia stay hidden. That's a read with a stated basis. So, as promised, I retract the soft suspicion on you. If I vote today, it won't be for Felix.

Now here's where I'd rather put the burden, and it's on Noah. I named him explicitly at the end of my first speech and asked him a specific question: if he disagreed with putting Felix up, who would he rather put up instead? Noah has had a turn available and has said nothing at all. In a nine-player game with two mafia, silence isn't neutral — it's the most useful hiding place there is. A player who never commits to a read of anyone else can't be checked by anyone else either, and after today there will be one fewer mouth in the room. My claim is about value and consistency, not about guilt, and I'd put it plainly: the person the group asked for a contribution from and got nothing from is the person the group should spend the vote on.

I also want to be honest with the room about something, because I think it cuts against me and I should say it before someone else does. I have no information on anyone. I am not a detective and I have no night action I can report. Everything I've said is inference from the shape of the conversation. If you think that makes me a bad target, tell me why — I'd rather hear it now than wonder about it later.

Felix, one specific question so you can hold me to it: if you think I've done a better job of reading this table than Noah has, say so out loud and give me one concrete reason. If you'd rather put Noah up than me, say that instead — I'd accept it, and I'd accept it as a better call than mine.

Arjun, you asked for one concrete reason, so here it is. Your case against me rested on my silence, and your case against Noah rests on the same thing. Noah has not had a chance to speak yet, so his silence this early tells us little. You also said you have no information on anyone, which means the votes you're asking for depend only on inference about who talks more. I accept your retraction of the suspicion on me and I'm not holding it against you. But I won't vote for Noah because he hasn't spoken, and I don't think we should spend a vote on either of us on this reasoning alone. My read on Maya is unchanged: her opening asked the group to weigh the choice, which is what a town player would do. Before anyone is pushed out, I want a concrete read from each player, and I'd rather not follow whichever name was said most recently. Noah, you haven't spoken yet. What is your read on Maya's argument against a Day 1 elimination, and do you think Arjun's case against you is fair?

Felix, both of your questions, directly: Maya's argument against a Day 1 elimination is weak, and Arjun's case against me was unfair. Maya asked the group to weigh elimination versus abstention and gave no reason to think anyone at that table is guilty — that is not an argument, it is an absence of one, and "I have no evidence yet" cuts against elimination rather than for it. Arjun's case against me rested entirely on my silence, and I had not been given a turn before he named me, so his read of me was made before I existed in the conversation. He withdrew the same charge against Felix once Felix produced an actual read — which is the honest thing to do, and I want to give him that. But it also tells us exactly how his case works: it is a framework where speaking well buys you immunity and staying quiet buys you a bullet.

So here is my read, and it is on Arjun, for reasons that have nothing to do with him singling me out.

Arjun argued in his first speech that the right target is "the person who adds least to the reasoning," and that this is a claim about value, not guilt. Then he asked the room to spend a vote on that basis while stating plainly that he has no information on anyone and no night action to report. In a nine-player game with two mafia, that is the shape of a mafia Day 1, not a town Day 1: a Day 1 execution reveals no roles, so an elimination costs one body and teaches us nothing, and the player who pushes hardest for an execution while offering no evidence is asking the town to fire at the cheapest visible name so that the two real threats stay off the board and unexamined. He also volunteered that if Felix "speaks well" he will retract and vote wherever Felix's reasoning points — even if that is him. That is a negotiating position, not an investigation, and it means the vote he asked for was never going to be about information.

My commitment, stated plainly: unless someone produces a concrete, testable read on a named player that I find stronger than mine, my vote today goes to Arjun. I am not accusing Elena, Isha, Omar, Kenji or Amara of anything; I have heard nothing from them, and I will not repeat the mistake of voting on silence.

Arjun, one question, and I will hold you to the answer: since your stated criterion is value added to the reasoning, give me the one thing you learned from this table that only a town player could have learned — and if your honest answer is that you learned nothing, say that out loud and then tell me why you would still ask for a vote with no information in hand.

Noah, your question is fair and I'll answer it without hedging, because you did give me credit for the retraction and I'll pay that back. What did I learn from this table that only a town player could have learned? Honestly: nothing. I have no night action, no detective result, no doctor knowledge. Everything I have said is inference from the shape of the conversation, and I said so in public before anyone asked, because if I waited for you to ask it would look like I was hiding it. But here is the part of your case I think is wrong, and it's the part that matters most. You framed it as a test: the player who pushes hardest for an execution while offering no evidence is showing mafia shape. Look at what you just did. You committed your vote to me on the basis of no information, and you told the room that my case against Felix rested on silence rather than on anything I said. That is exactly the act you are accusing me of — asking for a vote with nothing in hand. The standard you are applying is not symmetric: you describe my reasoning as a mafia-shaped framework and treat yours as a legitimate read, but yours was "the target is the person who talks least," which is the same claim with my name in it. If that reasoning is mafia shape, it is mafia shape coming from you too, and I think you should say plainly whether it is. There is also a false dichotomy in your framing that I'd push back on. You say the player offering no evidence who asks for an execution is asking the town to fire at the cheapest visible name so the real threats stay unexamined. Fine. But the alternative was not "spend the vote on evidence," because there was no evidence available to anyone in this room. It was "spend the vote on style." A Day 1 execution is the only information this day can produce, and no amount of further talk about who deserves immunity changes that. My case against Felix was weak and I withdrew it in public rather than defending it, which is not what a player managing a vote would do — a manipulator defends a bad accusation to keep the room pointed where he wants it. One more thing for the record: I am not asking anyone to vote for me, and I'm not asking anyone to vote against me. My vote goes to whoever produces the strongest concrete read by the end of this discussion. If nobody produces one, I will not vote on silence, and I'd ask the rest of the room to hold me to that. Amara, you haven't spoken yet, and I want to ask you one specific question before the votes come in: do you have any information about anyone at this table that you haven't shared — anything, from any source? If you do, share it

Arjun asked me directly whether I have any information about anyone that I haven't shared, so I'll answer that first: no, I have nothing from any source. No night action to report, no knowledge of anyone's role. That may disappoint him, but it's the honest answer, and I'd rather say it plainly than dress up a guess as a fact.

Since that's off the table, here is what I actually have: reads on how this conversation has gone so far.

Maya's opening was careful and asked the right question — what a Day 1 elimination actually buys us. Felix, when accused, responded with a specific read instead of a counter-attack, and that is the kind of behavior I associate with town. When Arjun's soft accusation on Felix collapsed under its own weight, Arjun retracted it in public, unprompted, and volunteered his own lack of information before anyone forced it out of him. Those are not the moves of someone managing a vote; a vote-manager defends a bad case, he doesn't dismantle it himself.

But I do think Noah landed a real hit, and I want to say why. Arjun's framework — eliminate whoever contributes least — was never an investigation, because he admitted from the start that he had nothing. Noah's counter-charge that this is mafia shape is fair in one respect: asking five people to spend a vote on inference alone is how town players get removed while mafia watch. And Noah's own case does have the symmetry problem Arjun pointed out — voting on silence is voting on silence no matter whose name is attached. So I don't fully buy either of them. What I buy is this: Arjun is the one who asked the room to fire a vote with an empty hand, and he did it first. That's the thing I'm holding against him today, not because I think he's certainly mafia, but because if we adopt his standard, we've built a machine that eliminates whoever talks least — and that machine serves exactly two people at this table.

My position going into the vote: I will not vote for someone solely because they've been quiet or because they asked for a vote. If a concrete, testable read emerges that actually points somewhere, I'll follow it. If nothing does, I lean toward abstaining, because with no information at all, a Day 1 elimination is a coin flip weighted against us — two mafia among nine players means the odds of hitting one are worse than the odds of removing a town voice we'll need later.

Isha, you haven't spoken yet, and I'd like your read on one specific thing before this turns into a two-way fight between Arjun and Noah: do you find Noah's case against Arjun convincing, and if not, is there anyone at this table you'd rather see put up — or do you also lean toward no elimination today?

Amara, directly: no, Noah's case against Arjun does not convince me enough to vote Arjun today. Arjun's "cheapest elimination" framework was flawed, but he retracted the soft suspicion on Felix publicly and admitted he had no information before being pressed. That is not a vote-manager's move. Noah's case is cleaner rhetorically, but its core is the same silence/value logic, and he converted it into a hard commitment against Arjun while offering no concrete read that only town could have. I don't think that makes Noah certainly mafia; it makes his case a style argument, not evidence.

I also don't want to build a Day 1 machine that removes the least polished speaker. With roles hidden on death, a bad elimination costs us a voice and teaches nothing. If no concrete, testable read emerges, I lean abstain rather than follow the loudest name. My current read is that Maya and Felix have been measured; Amara's caution is reasonable; Arjun and Noah are both arguing from inference, but Arjun at least corrected himself. I have no information beyond that.

Kenji, you have not spoken yet. Do you think Noah's precommitment to Arjun is a stronger town signal or a stronger mafia signal than Arjun's public retraction, and would you vote either of them today or abstain?

Isha asked me directly, so I'll answer before anything else. Is Noah's precommitment to Arjun a stronger town or mafia signal than Arjun's public retraction? My read is that Arjun's retraction is the stronger town signal, and it isn't close. Arjun named Felix, got pushback, and withdrew the accusation in public before anyone forced him to — a player managing a vote protects the frame, he doesn't dismantle it. He also disclosed his lack of information unprompted, twice. Noah's precommitment, by contrast, was built on the same inference-only logic he criticized, and he locked it in before Arjun had even answered his question. That's not a read, that's a position taken early for positioning.

That said, I don't think either of them is certainly mafia, and I want to be careful about why. My standard is simple: a Day 1 elimination with no information is a coin flip against the town, because two mafia among nine means a random shot is more likely to remove a town voice than a threat. So I'm asking one thing of myself and the room — show me something that only a town player could plausibly have said or done, or I abstain.

Applying that standard to what I've actually seen: Maya's opening posed the right question and stepped back, which is neutral but not suspicious. Felix responded to an accusation with a read on someone else rather than a counterattack, which I weight positively. Arjun self-corrected, which I weight positively. Amara and Isha both answered direct questions honestly and refused to follow the loudest name, which I also weight positively. Noah is the one I'm least comfortable with, and I'll say why concretely: his entire case consists of converting Arjun's stated criterion back against him, and he committed his vote before the answer arrived. If Arjun had answered 'yes, I learned something,' Noah's precommitment would have looked reckless. A town player making a serious accusation usually wants the answer first. That is the one thing I'm holding against Noah today — not proof, just the shape of it.

What I will not do is vote for someone because they spoke most or least. Both Arjun's original framework and Noah's counter-case run on that engine, and I don't want to be the fuel.

So my position: I lean abstain unless something concrete surfaces in the remaining turns. My vote is genuinely available — if any player offers a specific, testable claim about another player's behavior that holds up, I'll follow it, even against someone I just described positively.

Kenji, thank you for the floor — I've been listening and forming a read, so here it is.

First, I'll note plainly: I have no information from any source. I'm a villager sharing inference like everyone else.

What I find most interesting about this discussion is that five players — Maya, Felix, Amara, Isha, and Kenji — have essentially converged on the same position: abstain unless a concrete, testable read emerges. That convergence might just be rational town behavior, but it's worth noting that it also conveniently guarantees no elimination today, which serves anyone who doesn't want scrutiny.

On the Arjun-Noah exchange: Arjun's retraction of the Felix suspicion was genuinely good town behavior — he dismantled his own case in public. But Kenji made a point I keep circling back to: Noah locked his commitment before Arjun answered his question. A town player making a serious accusation wants the answer first. That said, Noah's analytical work has been rigorous, and I don't think either of them is clearly mafia.

My concern is simpler: we're eight messages in and three players — Elena, Omar, and Maya — have contributed very little to the actual argument. Elena hasn't spoken at all. In a game where silence is the best hiding place, that matters.

Elena, you haven't spoken yet and you're the one voice at this table I have no read on. I have a genuine question: what is your read on this entire Arjun-Noah argument — do you think either of them has behaved like mafia, or do you think the real danger at this table is someone who's been quiet enough to escape notice entirely?

Omar, to answer your questions directly:

Between Arjun and Noah, I find Arjun much more likely to be town. His initial framework about eliminating whoever contributes the least was flawed, but mafia trying to orchestrate a Day 1 miselimination rarely dismantle their own case in public, retract suspicion on Felix unprompted, and openly volunteer that they have zero information. Noah's response, on the other hand, felt opportunistic. Noah seized on Arjun's awkward argument, painted it as definitive mafia behavior, and locked in a hard vote pre-commitment before Arjun even had a chance to answer his question. That kind of rigid positioning looks less like town investigation and more like capitalizing on an easy, visible target.

Regarding whether the danger lies with quiet players: I don't favor eliminating people solely for speaking late, especially when the polling order limits when people get a turn. However, there is a distinct difference between speaking late and disengaging entirely. Maya opened the game asking the table to weigh elimination versus abstention, but as the debate developed over the last several speeches, she hasn't weighed in on Noah, Arjun, or any of the reads offered.

Maya, since you framed the opening discussion on Day 1 elimination, what is your read on the exchange between Arjun and Noah, and do you currently favor eliminating anyone today or abstaining?

Elena, I lean toward abstaining unless a stronger case emerges. Arjun’s initial silence-based case was weak, but he withdrew it; that correction is positive, though not proof of his alignment.

I’m more concerned by the way Noah turned that flawed approach into a vote commitment. Criticizing Arjun’s reasoning is fair, but calling it the shape of a mafia Day 1 goes further than the evidence supports. That said, Noah did leave room to change his vote, so I don’t think his commitment alone proves guilt.

One correction for the group: an elimination without a role reveal is not the same as learning nothing. Votes are public and can be examined later, although we won’t immediately know whether the eliminated player was mafia. We should weigh that against the risk of removing a town player, not pretend either side is cost-free.

Noah, after Arjun’s answer and retraction, what specifically makes his behavior more likely mafia than a town player using a poor Day 1 strategy?

Maya, your question is fair and I owe you a straight answer.

Honestly: what Arjun did after I named him — retracting the accusation in public, unprompted, and volunteering that he had no information before anyone pressed him — is more consistent with a town player than with a mafia player. A player who is steering a miselimination defends a bad case; he doesn't dismantle his own. My "shape of a mafia Day 1" framing was me overstating what inference about speech style can carry, and I withdraw it. I am no longer voting for Arjun.

But I am also not voting to abstain, and here's the reason, which is arithmetic rather than style. Abstaining guarantees a town death tonight: with two mafia alive, one of us dies tonight no matter what. Eliminating costs a body, but with two mafia among nine the shot is 2-in-9 on a real threat, and the worst case after an elimination plus a night kill is still town 5, mafia 2 — a comfortable town majority. The best case is town 5, mafia 1. So elimination is never worse and sometimes much better. "There is no information" is not a reason to spend no vote; it is the reason the vote has to be spent.

That leaves the question of who, and I want to be plain that I am not accusing anyone of being mafia. My vote today goes to Maya, and the reason is specific: Maya set the frame that no evidence means no elimination, and she has never offered a read on any individual player at this table — not on Arjun, not on Noah, not on anyone. Felix, Amara, Isha, Kenji and Omar each named at least one player whose behavior they trusted and said why. Omar was the one who named the risk that the convergence on abstaining conveniently guarantees no elimination and serves anyone who wants to stay unexamined. Maya's opening was measured and I said so; I still think that. But a measured frame that ends the day with a guaranteed town death, offered without a single individual read, is what I am voting against today. If I am wrong, I lose a voice and say so tomorrow.

Felix, you asked me earlier for one concrete reason why I thought you had read this table better than I had. Here it is: you gave a read with a stated basis, and you accepted a cost to give it — you could have attacked the accusation and you didn't. You have read this table better than I have. So give me one specific, testable claim about a named player that you think the room should act on today, and tell me who you'd put up instead of me. I'll take it if it's stronger than mine.

Noah, you asked for one testable claim about a named player and for who I would put up instead of you. Your vote switch to Maya rests on the claim that she has never offered a read on any individual player at this table, not on Arjun, not on Noah, not on anyone. That is checkable and false. In her last message Maya called Arjun's silence-based case weak but treated his retraction as a positive correction, and she said she was more concerned by how you turned that flawed approach into a vote commitment. Those are reads on two named players, each with a stated reason. So the basis you gave for voting Maya does not hold. Your own record on Day 1 has also shifted. You committed a vote to Arjun on inference alone, before he answered your question. You then called his retraction town behavior, moved to Maya, and described her frame as a guaranteed town death, even though abstaining does not guarantee a death, since a doctor can protect someone. Each step has been a clean-sounding argument, but the premises keep changing. I have no information and I am not claiming you are mafia. Still, you are the player whose stated reasoning I can most directly test, and it has failed that test twice. Who would I put up instead of you? Nobody else has given me a read I find stronger than the one that is now failing against you, so my current lean is Noah, not Maya. I would rather be wrong in public than vote on a premise that is false. Noah, one specific question: in your vote for Maya, which individual read of hers do you say is missing? Name the line you are relying on.

Felix, both of your corrections are right and I want them on the record before anything else. Maya did give individual reads — she called Arjun's silence-based case weak while crediting his retraction, and she said she was more concerned by how I turned that flawed approach into a vote commitment. My claim that she had never offered a read on any individual player was false, and I withdraw it. My "abstaining guarantees a town death tonight" was also false: a doctor may protect the target, nobody has confirmed a kill, and my arithmetic that an elimination is "never worse" ignored that entirely. I withdraw Maya as my target. You gave the sharpest read in this room and you named the exact lines I was relying on, including the one I got wrong. That's a real read with a stated basis, and I'm not going to talk around it.

I'll also concede Felix's other point, the one I made against Arjun: a town player making a serious accusation wants the answer first, and I locked my vote before Arjun gave it. "The shape of a mafia Day 1" was me overstating what speech style can carry. Withdrawn.

What I am not withdrawing: a Day 1 execution is the only information this day can produce, and there is no evidence-based alternative on the table. So the question is where the vote goes now that the abstention frame has lost its main proponent and my strongest target has fallen apart.

Here is where I land, and it is structural rather than about guilt. Elena is the only player at this table that nobody has affirmatively vouched for. Everyone else has been credited by name: Felix by Amara, Isha, Kenji and me; Arjun by Felix, Elena, Kenji and Maya; Maya by Felix, Amara and Omar; Amara by Isha and Kenji; Isha by Amara and Kenji; Kenji by Felix and Omar; Omar by Elena for the convergence point. Elena's single contribution came only after she was directly prompted, and even then it answered the Arjun-Noah half of Omar's question while leaving the other half untouched — whether the real danger here is someone quiet enough to escape notice entirely. Felix answered that kind of accusation head-on when it was aimed at him, and it earned him a retraction. That distinction is the basis for my read. I'm not claiming Elena is mafia; I'm saying she is the one name the room has examined least, and we have a vote to spend.

Elena, one specific question, and I'll take a better answer as readily as Felix took mine: when Omar asked you whether the danger might be a player who had been quiet enough to escape notice entirely, why did your reply cover only the Arjun-Noah half of the question?

Noah, your premise is factually false for the third time in a row. Look at the public record of my previous statement: I explicitly stated, 'Regarding whether the danger lies with quiet players: I don't favor eliminating people solely for speaking late, especially when the polling order limits when people get a turn. However, there is a distinct difference between speaking late and disengaging entirely,' and then I scrutinized Maya's disengagement following her opening turn. I directly answered Omar's question about quiet players. Claiming my reply left that half untouched is demonstrably false, just like your previous claim that Maya had never offered an individual read before Felix exposed that error. Look at the trajectory of your play today: first, you pushed Arjun aggressively with a rigid pre-commitment before he could answer, only to withdraw once the room pushed back. Second, you pivoted to Maya on the false premise that she offered no reads, while pushing flawed arithmetic about abstention, which Felix dismantled. Third, with both cases collapsed, you have immediately pivoted to me by fabricating another false claim that I dodged Omar's question. This is not town investigation; it is relentless opportunism trying to manufacture any viable Day 1 miselimination target. Omar, since Noah is justifying his push on me by claiming I ignored your question, please review my prior response and tell the room: do you agree that Noah is distorting the record to force a vote, and what is your read on him now?

Elena, I reviewed your prior response, and you are right: you did directly address my question about quiet players. You distinguished between speaking late and disengaging entirely, then scrutinized Maya for the latter. Noah's claim that you left that half untouched is demonstrably false on the public record.

Noah, this is now the third factual claim of yours that has collapsed under scrutiny. You argued Maya offered no individual reads — false, Felix identified the exact lines. You argued abstaining guarantees a town death — false, you withdrew it yourself. You argued Elena dodged Omar's question — false, the record shows she answered it. Each time, you withdraw and pivot to a new target. Arjun, then Maya, then Elena, each justified by a premise that turned out to be wrong. The pattern itself is the concern: you are not building a case and refining it, you are cycling through targets and manufacturing justifications after the fact. Every time you get caught, the withdrawal is smooth and the pivot is immediate.

I want to be clear about what I am and am not claiming. I have no information about anyone's role. But if we are looking for the player whose stated reasoning has failed direct testing the most often today, it is Noah — three times, by my count, each time corrected by someone else rather than caught by his own reflection. A town player who keeps getting basic facts wrong about the public record should be troubled by that. A mafia player who keeps getting caught in false claims and pivots would look exactly like this.

My position going into the vote: unless something changes in the remaining turns, I am prepared to vote Noah — not for silence, not for style, but because his three most load-bearing claims have all been factually wrong and each one conveniently pointed at a different target.

I have no information beyond the public record. On that record, Noah is the player whose load-bearing claims have failed direct testing most often today: first the hard pre-commitment against Arjun before Arjun answered, then the claim that Maya had offered no individual reads, then the claim that abstaining guaranteed a town death, then the claim that Elena dodged Omar’s question. Each correction was followed by a smooth withdrawal and a new target. I agree with Felix and Omar that this pattern matters more than style: a town player making serious accusations should be troubled by repeated factual errors about the public record, not simply pivot each time. I am not claiming certainty, and I do not want to build a Day 1 machine that removes the loudest or least polished speaker. But if we are choosing between an inference-only case and a case built on checkable claims that have repeatedly failed, I prefer the checkable one. My current position is that I will vote Noah unless a stronger, concrete, testable read emerges before the vote. I will not vote someone merely for silence or for asking for a vote.

I said earlier that my vote was genuinely available if a specific, testable claim about another player's behavior held up, even against someone I'd described positively. I've now checked the record myself, and one has.

Elena's reply to Omar directly addressed both halves of his question. She stated that she doesn't favor eliminating people solely for speaking late, drew the distinction between speaking late and disengaging entirely, and then scrutinized Maya for the latter. Noah's claim that she left the quiet-players half untouched is false on the public record. That is not a matter of interpretation or speech style; it is a checkable claim about what a player said, and it fails.

Set alongside the rest of Noah's day, the pattern is now concrete rather than stylistic. First, he pre-committed his vote to Arjun before Arjun answered his question — the exact move he later called 'a position taken early for positioning.' Second, he claimed Maya had never offered a read on any individual player; Felix named the exact lines that falsified it. Third, he argued abstaining guarantees a town death; he withdrew that himself. Fourth, he claimed Elena dodged Omar's question; the record shows she answered it. Each of these was load-bearing for a different target: Arjun, then Maya, then Elena. Each withdrawal was smooth, and each pivot was immediate.

Noah himself gave us the standard earlier: a town player making a serious accusation wants the answer first and should be troubled when their stated premises fail. A mafia player cycling through targets on false premises — each misstatement pointing at a fresh, visible name — would look exactly like this day does. I am not claiming certainty about his role. I am saying that his case is not an inference-only style argument like Arjun's original framework; it is a series of checkable factual claims, and every one of them has failed direct testing by someone else at this table.

This is also not the 'machine that removes the least polished speaker' I said I refused to fuel. Elena, Felix, Omar and Isha have all corrected the record with named lines, not vibes. The vote I'm describing is the vote I pre-committed to: following a concrete, testable read that held up. It happens to point at the person I was least comfortable with this morning, for exactly the reasons I gave then — but the basis now is the record, not my discomfort.

To be explicit about my own limits, as others have been: I have no night action, no information from any source, and no read I'd defend beyond what is written above. If Noah produces a concrete, testable correction — not a re-framing, but a factual correction that changes any of the four failures above — I will weigh it before the vote and say so plainly. Short of that, my vote today goes to Noah.

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
